meta.title: Who really said "Even If You Win the Rat Race, You're Still a Rat"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The rat-race quip was in print by 1956, years before a 1971 graffiti anthology recorded it on a wall. Its coiner is unknown; Lily Tomlin popularized it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Even If You Win the Rat Race, You're Still a Rat'?
meta.ogDescription: In print by 1956 and recorded as graffiti in 1971. Nobody knows who coined it. Lily Tomlin made it famous, and Banksy and Coffin are also credited.

answer.label: Not graffiti in origin — an anonymous 1950s quip
answer.sourceLine: The joke was already in print in 1956. A wall-writing version, “Remember, even if you win the rat race—you’re still a rat,” was collected in Robert Reisner’s 1971 anthology Graffiti: Two Thousand Years of Wall Writing. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the quip “was in circulation by 1956” and does not name a coiner. Graffiti passed it along; graffiti did not invent it.

source.excerpt: Remember, even if you win the rat race—you’re still a rat.
trail: 1956 — Jim Bishop’s The Golden Ham: A Candid Biography of Jackie Gleason prints a Gleason letter: “Television is a rat race, and remember this, even if you win you are still a rat.” This is the earliest appearance known to Quote Investigator ↗.
11 Aug 1956 — In the Boston Herald, Bill Cunningham writes, “like the fellow said, ‘You can win the rat race, but you’re still a rat,’” and claims no credit for it (Barry Popik ↗).

1965 — William Sloane Coffin Jr., writing in Life, quotes a student: “And even if you win a rat race, you’re still a rat.” Russell Baker uses the line in a newspaper satire the same year (Quote Investigator ↗).

1971 & 1977 — Reisner’s Graffiti records the wall version. Then People (26 Dec 1977) quotes Lily Tomlin: “The trouble with the rat race is that even if you win you’re still a rat” (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the graffito as Quote Investigator transcribes it from Reisner’s 1971 compilation. The anthology recorded wall writing; it does not say who wrote the line or where it came from.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About Anonymous
author.bio: Nobody has identified who first said this. Quote Investigator finds it in 1956: in a Jackie Gleason letter printed in Jim Bishop’s biography The Golden Ham, and in a Boston Herald sports column where Bill Cunningham credited “the fellow.” The joke later reached walls, sermons and stand-up comedy. Lily Tomlin, who took it into the 1970s mainstream, is the name most often attached to it.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: The joke is anonymous, so it has collected a long list of authors. Some people really used it. None of them can be shown to have coined it.

items.why: A graffito version appears in Robert Reisner’s 1971 Graffiti anthology. By then the quip had been in print for more than a decade (Quote Investigator ↗).

People quoted her in December 1977, and QI calls her “an important vector for its popularization.” QI also says she used the jest only after it had spread (Quote Investigator ↗). Wikiquote lists her version under material credited to her writer Jane Wagner (Wikiquote ↗).

Coffin thought he may have coined it as a chaplain in the 1950s or 1960s. QI calls the evidence for this “weak,” and in his 1965 Life piece he put the line in a student’s mouth (Quote Investigator ↗).
Gleason applied it to television in a letter printed in 1956. QI says it is not clear whether he ever used it on stage (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote sites credit “You can win the rat race but you’re still a rat” to the street artist and give no public source (Quotewise ↗). The joke was in print by 1956, so it is older than his career, and he probably got the credit because the line is linked to graffiti.

misattribution.truthLine: No coiner is known. The quip was “in circulation by 1956,” graffiti recorded it in 1971, and Lily Tomlin made it famous (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: “Rat race” was mid-century slang for a pointless competitive grind. Wikipedia dates its figurative sense to 1939 (Wikipedia ↗). The punchline takes the metaphor literally: winning does not get you out of it.

A one-liner with no owner moves easily from columnists to campus chaplains, onto walls and into stand-up. Each new voice gets credited along the way. That is why graffiti, Tomlin, Coffin, Gleason and Banksy all show up as “the author” of a joke that none of them can be shown to have invented.
